families.name: New Rust Project
instructions: Start an original Rust application, service, library, or tool. Determine its concrete intended workflows and interfaces before choosing binary, library, workspace or multi-crate layout; do not scaffold unnecessary crates.

Choose the currently supported stable Rust edition and minimum supported toolchain according to project policy. Prefer standard library and well-maintained Rust crates; document nontrivial dependencies and MIT-first licensing decisions.

Track implementation, unit/integration/edge-case tests, cargo fmt, Clippy, CI, runtime validation on target platforms, packaging, documentation, and release readiness as appropriate. Evaluate actual user-facing operation, not merely compilation.
Build on main by default unless a project-specific branch rule applies. Keep scope fixed to authorized features and report evidence-backed progress.

families.name: Rust Port (Any Source Language)
instructions: Treat the upstream application's specified baseline as the behavioral specification. Identify the exact upstream repository, version/commit, supported platforms, executable/library entrypoints, APIs, CLI options, formats, persistent data, external integrations, and error behavior.

Create a traceable upstream capability inventory and full parity matrix with explicit supported, missing, blocked, and verified states. Make user-visible parity and independently runnable replacement capability the default MVP acceptance criteria, not architectural resemblance or code-volume parity.

Use differential or golden tests against a reference implementation when available, plus real target-environment checks. Preserve compatibility and document justified deviations; do not add speculative improvements before parity.
Investigate source-license and dependency obligations before importing code; MIT is preferred only when compatible. Count integration and hard-to-port edge cases in the original progress baseline.

families.name: Independent Public Tarium Project
instructions: Build a self-sufficient, independently published public Tarium project in its own repository. The central Tarium repository is a registry/governance hub, never a monorepo hosting member implementation or datasets.

Establish a coherent domain ontology in human-readable docs and machine-readable form. Develop an accessible public showcase/gallery, machine-readable gallery index, source/provenance and validation, with functioning Day/Night/System appearance controls.

Treat privacy and public provenance as release blockers: do not migrate or reveal private Taria materials, private conversations, credentials, research inputs, or unpublished work. Independently reconstruct public-safe specimens and citations as needed.

Do not enroll this repository in public Tarium or modify the hub without separate explicit named-project authorization. Plan website, ontology integrity, gallery references, licensing, packaging and deployment from the beginning.

families.name: Rust Fork Maintenance
instructions: Identify upstream repository, current upstream revision, the selected fork baseline, compatible APIs, and the reason for maintaining the fork. Preserve the existing fork identity and changes.

Inventory and label fork-owned patches, upstream fixes, local deviations, synchronization decisions and compatibility commitments. Track divergence with concrete upstream commits and assess conflicts before integration.
Choose upstream imports only when in scope, preserve intentional fork behavior, and verify affected behavior, public APIs, build targets, regression tests, CI, and actual downstream use.
Do not silently replace fork-specific code, force-push history or upgrade dependencies without authorization. Maintain clear provenance and release compatibility records.

families.name: C → Rust Port
instructions: Record compiler dialect/options, platform ABIs, binary boundaries, preprocessor conditions, pointer aliasing, manual allocation, structures/unions, integer/overflow behavior, concurrency and undefined-behavior hazards.
Map each upstream C component to a verified Rust replacement, maintaining byte-level/behavioral compatibility where required. Keep unsafe Rust and FFI tightly scoped, justified, and tested.
Run differential C/Rust tests and real operating-system checks for file formats, CLI, API, resource handling and failure paths. Do not equate compiling with parity.

families.name: C++ → Rust Port
instructions: Inventory the upstream C++ standard, templates, class hierarchies, virtual dispatch, ownership and lifetime contracts, STL container behavior, exceptions, RTTI, threads, ABI/FFI interfaces, macros, and build flags as applicable.
Specify equivalent Rust representations without accidentally changing observable behavior or serialized formats. Make compatibility decisions and any justified non-parity explicit.
Use differential behavior and fixture tests, edge/error-path coverage, platform builds, integration and downstream consumer checks; verify actual replacement capability before declaring parity.

families.name: Python → Rust Port
instructions: Identify upstream Python version, interpreter-specific behavior, package/runtime entrypoints, exceptions, iteration and truthiness semantics, dynamic types, serialization, async scheduling and dependency behavior that affect outputs.

Inventory every in-scope module, CLI/API surface, plugin/extension compatibility, network/file behaviors and error cases. Implement idiomatic Rust while retaining agreed user-visible parity, not Python internals as an end in themselves.

Compare Rust and reference Python behavior with reproducible fixtures and differential tests, including malformed inputs and integration endpoints. Mark unsupported or intentionally changed behavior explicitly.
